text:
This guidance explains how specified public authorities can charge and recover costs for services provided in relation to certain applications, orders and schemes under the Highways Act 1980 and the Transport and Works Act 1992.

It sets out:

which public authorities can charge fees

which services fees can be charged for

how fees may be calculated and paid

information public authorities must publish before charging fees

what happens if fees are disputed or remain unpaid

The guidance supports the operation of the Transport Infrastructure (Fees) Regulations 2026 and must be read alongside the regulations.

Introduction

The Transport Infrastructure (Fees) Regulations 2026 (the regulations) have been introduced to support timely and effective engagement between specified public authorities and highway authorities under the Highways Act 1980 (HA80), and applicants under the Transport and Works Act 1992 (TWA).

The regulations do this by enabling the specified public authorities to charge fees to recover the costs they incur in providing relevant services. These services must relate to specific HA80 orders and schemes, or to TWA applications.

The anticipated benefits of cost recovery are most likely to be realised where the parties involved engage openly from an early stage and maintain that engagement throughout the process.

The decision to implement cost recovery powers is discretionary. The specified public authorities can choose not to implement them or implement them at a later date.

Where cost recovery powers are implemented, the regulations provide the framework for their operation and administration. The regulations include a number of mandatory requirements which must be complied with. Beyond these requirements, the specified public authorities retain discretion over how they implement and administer their cost recovery arrangements.

This guidance is statutory. Public authorities must have regard to it when exercising functions under the regulations. This guidance should be read alongside the regulations. It does not replace the regulations and is not a substitute for professional or legal advice where issues are technical, complex or unclear.

The explanatory memorandum that accompanies the regulations provides further details on the statutory framework and policy rationale.

Public authorities that can charge fees for relevant services

The public authorities that can charge fees under the regulations are:

The Coal Authority

The Environment Agency

The Health and Safety Executive

The Historic Buildings and Monuments Commission for England

Local authorities in England

The Marine Management Organisation

Natural England

National Highways

Transport for London

Where the relevant services are provided in connection with an application for a cross-border order under the TWA, the public authorities that can charge fees under the regulations are those already listed above, and:

Natural Resources Wales

Welsh Ministers

Local authorities in Wales

Who the public authorities can recover costs from

The public authorities can charge fees for relevant services provided to the following parties.

Highway authorities (as defined in section 1 of the Highways Act 1980)

When in connection with an order made, or proposed to be made, under Part 2, 6 or 12 of the HA80, or a scheme made, or proposed to be made, under s16 or 106 of the HA80. Such orders or schemes may relate to, for example:

trunking and de-trunking roads

the stopping up/improvement of classified/trunk roads

the construction of bridges and tunnels over/under navigable waters

matters relating to acquisition, vesting and transfer of land

Applicants

When in connection with an application under section 6 of the TWA. Such orders may relate to, for example, the construction or operation of:

railways

tramways

trolley vehicle systems

other guided vehicle systems

inland waterways

Services fees can be charged for

Fees can be charged to highway authorities and applicants for relevant services. This means any advice, information or other assistance provided in connection with the schemes, orders and applications noted above.

Such services may include those listed below. These are illustrative examples and the list is not intended to be exhaustive or definitive:

responding to statutory or non-statutory consultations

providing technical advice, information or other assistance to support a scheme, order or application

reviewing and commenting on documents during the relevant stages of an order, scheme or application

attending meetings or workshops with a highway authority or applicant to discuss scheme development, likely impacts, mitigation or delivery issues

providing specialist input to help highway authorities or applicants understand the matters a public authority is likely to consider when exercising its statutory functions

The ability to charge for services does not create any new duty for a public authority to provide services outside its existing statutory functions or responsibilities. It does not require a public authority to provide additional advisory, pre-application or technical services beyond the role it would otherwise perform in relation to the relevant order, scheme or application.

Information public authorities must provide before charging fees

To be able to charge and recover fees for a relevant service, the public authority must have published a statement on its website which:

describes the relevant services for which fees are charged

refers to any legislative provisions under which the services are provided

sets out the fees, or the method by which the fees will be calculated

Public authorities which do not publish this information will not be able to charge fees under these regulations.

How fees will be set/calculated

The exact method by which the public authority sets and/or calculates fees is not prescribed by the regulations. However, there are 2 important principles in the regulations which determine and limit how fees must be set or calculated:

the fees can only be based on the cost to the public authority ‘of anything which is reasonably incidental to the provision’ of the relevant services

fees charged to a highway authority or applicant ‘must not exceed the costs reasonably incurred or to be incurred’ in providing the relevant services

Public authorities are encouraged to provide as clear and detailed information as possible about the fees they set and/or the methods they use to calculate them.

They should consider how the information in Understanding likely costs and fees may factor into the fee information they provide, through either the published statement on their website, and/or through their communications and/or working arrangements with highway authorities and applicants.

Understanding likely costs and fees

The public authorities must set out the fees for their services, or the method by which the fees will be calculated, on their website. Public authorities are encouraged to make clear what their service offerings cover and to set out any limits on the advice or assistance they can or will provide.

The actual costs of the services provided by the public authorities are likely to vary on a case-by-case basis, subject to the work required. Costs may also change during the course of the work as circumstances change.

Highway authorities, applicants and the public authorities are encouraged to set out their expectations and agree the scope of any chargeable services before work starts. This is particularly important for larger or more complex matters. Both parties should maintain an open dialogue and provide updates on changing circumstances throughout.

The public authorities are not obliged to provide fee estimates. However, where proportionate and reasonably practicable, they are strongly encouraged to set out the likely costs of the services to be provided. This may include a breakdown of charges or a fee estimate, particularly where costs may vary depending on the work required, including any separate charges or disbursements that may arise during the work.

Where a public authority has chosen to provide a fee estimate, it may request that a highway authority or applicant agree to the estimate before starting the work.

Highway authorities and applicants are strongly encouraged to engage early with the public authorities and provide enough information to allow them to understand the extent of the services requested of them. Providing clear information at the outset can help the public authorities allocate resources, provide more accurate fee estimates (where they choose to do so), and give timely advice and support. Such information should include, where practicable:

the scope of the work

expected timescales

points in the process which the public authority should be aware of – for example, deadlines, inquiries or hearing dates, decision points on a project’s critical path, parallel consenting, or similar matters

anticipated risks to delivery

key environmental issues – for example, designated sites, protected species

key technical issues

any specific expectations of the public authority

a nominated contact to simplify communications, or where relevant and if helpful, contact details of any key specialists engaged with the work, such as consultants, planners, and/or technical experts

Payment of fees

Highway authorities and applicants should provide the public authority with sufficient contact details to allow fees for its services to be charged and recovered. This should include:

the correct entity to be charged

details of finance teams or other contacts dealing with invoicing

The exact information required may vary between public authorities. It is recommended that highway authorities and applicants check the relevant public authority’s requirements at the outset.

The public authority must issue a written notice of the fees being charged to the highway authority or applicant. The notice may specify a period for payment, which cannot be less than 21 days from the date of the notice. This notice is, in effect, an invoice for the amount due at that point, and so it is referred to as an ‘invoice’ for the remainder of this guidance.

The highway authority or applicant must pay the full amount of the invoice within the period specified.

Invoices can be issued at any time, including:

in advance of services being undertaken

on a regular or rolling basis

following the provision of the services

The public authorities have a wide range of discretion in how they practically administer fee payments for the services provided. They are not required to provide a breakdown of their invoices. To try and avoid disputes in the future however, they are encouraged to provide breakdowns where they judge it to be proportionate and reasonably practicable.

Similarly, they are encouraged to set out information clearly (for example, on their websites and/or in their invoices) in relation to administrative matters such as:

payment timeframes

how to make payments

fee calculations

The public authorities may:

break down their total fees into stages and issue multiple invoices over the course of the work

at their discretion, in accordance with a statement published on their website, agree to the payment of fees by instalments, and make provision for fee waivers or refunds

Where payment is to be made by instalments, the public authority should make clear when each payment is due. This may be done by setting out a schedule of instalment payments, provided the highway authority or applicant receives at least 21 days’ notice before any payment is required.

If a future scheduled payment date or amount changes and the public authority issues a new invoice accordingly, the public authority must ensure the highway authority or applicant receives at least 21 days’ notice before the revised payment is due.

The public authority can require all or part of the fees to be paid in advance of work being undertaken, in accordance with a statement published on its website. Where they do so, they should keep the amount charged under review against the costs reasonably incurred or to be incurred in providing the relevant service. If the amount paid exceeds the costs that may be recovered under the regulations, the public authority must adjust the fee accordingly. This may include refunding all or part of the fee, where appropriate, in accordance with the public authority’s published charging statement.

Disputes

There is no mechanism in the regulations for highway authorities or applicants to challenge the reasonableness of the fees presented in the invoice. This does not prevent public authorities from agreeing dispute resolution procedures with highway authorities or applicants.

Public authorities are encouraged to provide upfront estimates, updates and breakdowns of their fees where proportionate and reasonably practicable. Both parties are encouraged to engage openly and transparently throughout.

In the event of a dispute about the amount of a fee, the highway authority or applicant and the public authority are encouraged to seek to resolve it through early and constructive discussion, including by sharing relevant information about how the fee has been calculated.

Entering into discussions or any other form of dispute resolution does not prevent the public authorities from exercising their powers to withhold services for non-payment.

Consequences of non-payment

If a highway authority or applicant does not pay the required fee to the public authority in the period specified on the invoice, the public authority may:

in relation to a relevant service which has not yet commenced - withhold providing the service until the fee is paid

in relation to a relevant service which has been provided in full - recover any unpaid fees from the highway authority or applicant as a civil debt

in relation to a relevant service which has been provided in part, either or both of the following - withhold providing the remainder of the service until the fee is paid and/or recover any unpaid fees from the highway authority or applicant as a civil debt

Highway authorities and applicants should note that this is notwithstanding any statutory requirement to provide the relevant services.

Bringing the cost recovery powers into operation

When the specified public authorities can begin charging fees

The specified public authorities will be able to introduce cost recovery for relevant services provided from 20 November 2026.

Public authorities may only begin charging fees once they have published the required charging information on their website. They cannot charge fees for any relevant services provided before 20 November 2026, or in relation to current applications, orders or schemes that have reached a certain stage, as set out in the next section.

The position in relation to existing orders, schemes or applications

The regulations will not apply to orders, schemes or applications that have already reached the following stages before the regulations come into force:

for TWA applications, where the application has been submitted to the Secretary of State before 20 November 2026

for HA80 orders or schemes, where a notice publicising the order/scheme has first been published before 20 November 2026

This means that public authorities will not be able to recover fees under these regulations for services provided in relation to those orders, schemes or applications.

Cost recovery in different consenting regimes

The principles of cost recovery apply across many different planning and consenting regimes. Highway authorities, applicants and the public authorities should be aware of the charging frameworks and cost recovery arrangements that may apply to proposed developments over their lifetime.

Section 35B of the Planning Act 2008 provides for development that would otherwise require development consent to be considered through an alternative consenting regime where the Secretary of State is satisfied that the alternative regime is appropriate for the development. Further information on this process can be found in the guidance on powers to direct a project into or out of the NSIP regime, which identifies both HA80 and TWA as potential alternative consenting regimes.
